ea: Alberta votes on October eighteenth, twenty twenty-seven. Calgary elects twenty-six of the Legislature's eighty-seven members, and many of the province's closest seats are here. This is what the numbers say, for any candidate.

Thirteen of Calgary's twenty-six electoral divisions were won by less than five points. In Calgary-Acadia, the margin was twenty-two votes. In Calgary-Glenmore, forty-eight. In Calgary-North West, one hundred and forty-three.

In every division, the people who stayed home outnumber the winning margin. About three hundred and fifty thousand electors on Calgary's lists did not vote. In the Calgary-Shaw by-election this September, turnout was just thirty-six percent, and the seat changed hands by five hundred and ninety-one votes.

The October referendum is the newest map of local opinion. On each of the first nine questions, Calgary's Yes vote was seven to eight points below Alberta's. Eighty-two percent of Calgary voters chose for Alberta to remain a province, against seventy-five percent province-wide.

Where do voters get their news? Social media now leads television. For half of Canadians aged eighteen to thirty-four, it is the main source of news. YouTube and Facebook lead, then Instagram, TikTok and X. Only thirty-seven percent trust most news, so short, local video with a source goes furthest.

Young people vote less: sixty-six percent of eighteen to twenty-four year olds, against seventy-six percent of all Canadians. Registration, campus outreach, young volunteers, and plain information on how to vote close that gap, and they help every voter.

The playbook for any campaign: know the arithmetic. Map the lowest-turnout polling stations. Register and remind. Listen before you speak. Put local facts on every screen. And measure progress every week.

iv: Calgary: a hub of innovation, leadership and future growth. Here is what a new investor should know, with the numbers, and where they come from.

Calgary is home to about one point six million people. In the year to July twenty twenty-five, its metro area grew two point nine percent, among the fastest in Canada. Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal grew half a percent or less.

Alberta has Canada's lowest corporate income tax: eight percent provincial, twenty-three percent combined. There is no provincial sales tax, no payroll tax, and no health premium. Invest Alberta puts the advantage at sixteen point nine billion dollars this year.

Calgary is Canada's fastest-growing startup ecosystem. It ranks in the world's top fifty emerging ecosystems, worth seven billion dollars, with three point four billion in venture capital since twenty twenty-one, and a tech workforce up sixty-one percent in three years.

The infrastructure is already here. Calgary's airport carried a record nineteen point four million passengers in twenty twenty-five. Calgary is home to CPKC, the railway linking Canada, the United States and Mexico. And downtown has quality office space on competitive terms.

Where are the openings? Calgary has about six everyday local businesses for every thousand residents. In fast-growing suburbs like Cornerstone, Cityscape and Belmont, there are fewer than two. Grocery, health, child care and food are the clearest gaps.
Calgary is safer than the Canadian average, and far more affordable than Toronto or Vancouver. The risks to plan for: energy price cycles, high office vacancy, and a cooling housing market.
